meta.description: Not Carl Sagan. Newsweek reporter Sharon Begley wrote the line as the kicker of a 1977 profile of Sagan; his estate confirms he never said it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it to a 1977 Newsweek profile — the closing line was reporter Sharon Begley's, not Sagan's. His estate: he never said it.

answer.label: Not Carl Sagan — actually Sharon Begley
answer.sourceLine: The line is the closing sentence of “Seeking Other Worlds,” a Carl Sagan cover profile in Newsweek of 15 August 1977 — written by reporter Sharon Begley as the article’s kicker, and printed deliberately outside quotation marks because it was the magazine’s voice, not Sagan’s. Begley later confirmed it herself, and Sagan’s estate says he never wrote or spoke the words.

source.heading: The line in its real home: a magazine kicker

docMeta.dd: Sharon Begley — reporting team of David Gelman with Begley (New York), Dewey Gram (Los Angeles) and Evert Clark (Washington)
He is the article’s subject, not its author

source.excerpt: But no doubt, there are even stranger discoveries to be made . . . some totally new phenomenon perhaps . . . Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest known appearance to the final sentence of “Seeking Other Worlds,” a Sagan profile in Newsweek of 15 August 1977 (vol. 90, p. 53), and concludes that “based on current evidence Sagan did not create this quotation.”

The reporter herself settled it. On 13 January 2015 Sharon Begley told Quote Investigator, “The words were not Sagan’s,” explaining that Newsweek house style treated ending a story on a quote as lazy — writers were paid to craft an original, thought-provoking kicker (QI ↗). She confirmed to Check Your Fact ↗ that the saying was her own writing.

Sagan’s estate agrees. Pam Abbey of Druyan-Sagan Associates told Check Your Fact ↗: “Carl Sagan never wrote or spoke these words, nor would he” — adding that they were written by a Newsweek reporter profiling him in 1977. The fact-check’s verdict: False.

The misreading reached the White House. On 7 October 2009 President Obama told a National Medal of Science ceremony that Sagan “once described his enthusiasm for discovery in very simple terms. He said, ‘Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known’” (White House transcript ↗).
source.excerptNote: The tell is the punctuation. Sagan’s actual words elsewhere in the profile sit inside quotation marks; this closing passage does not. As Quote Investigator ↗ puts it, had Sagan spoken the line it would have been placed within such marks — instead it was written in a reportorial voice.

source.rightsNote: This is not a public-domain quotation. The sentence first appeared in “Seeking Other Worlds,” Newsweek, 15 August 1977 — a work published well after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, by an identifiable publisher and a named staff writer. Rights therefore rest with Newsweek and with Begley as author; nothing about the line’s long misattribution to Sagan changes that.

author.name: Sharon Begley
author.heading: The writer behind the words
author.bio: Sharon Begley joined Newsweek in 1977, one week after graduating from Yale, and spent roughly 25 years there becoming one of America’s most admired science writers. Over a 43-year career she also wrote for The Wall Street Journal, Reuters and STAT, and published books on neuroscience and brain plasticity; she died of lung cancer in January 2021, aged 64. Colleagues remembered her gift for making hard science vivid — a gift that, in her very first year on the job, produced a sentence the world has spent five decades giving to somebody else.

cite.sourceCitation: David Gelman with Sharon Begley, Dewey Gram, and Evert Clark, “Seeking Other Worlds,” Newsweek 90 (15 August 1977): 53. Earliest documented appearance; the closing sentence is the reporters’ kicker, printed without quotation marks, and is not a quotation of Carl Sagan. Origin established by Garson O’Toole, “Quote Origin: Somewhere, Something Incredible Is Waiting To Be Known,” Quote Investigator, 18 March 2013.

misattribution.heading: The fact-checker’s quote that failed its own fact-check
misattribution.intro: Few quotations have travelled further on worse paperwork. The line is pinned on Carl Sagan everywhere — posters, mugs, museum gift shops, presidential remarks — and it was never his. It is a magazine writer’s closing flourish that slipped its quotation marks and kept walking.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence that Sagan crafted the quotation, and concluded he did not create it. His estate is blunter: “Carl Sagan never wrote or spoke these words, nor would he” (Check Your Fact ↗).

items.scope: How it escaped into print as a quote
items.who: A 1982 newspaper columnist, then the Associated Press
items.why: Quote Investigator records an Illinois columnist publishing the line credited to Sagan in 1982, and the AP’s “Today in History” feature distributing it to newspapers as Sagan’s in 1988 — the wire-service moment that made it unstoppable (QI ↗).
At the National Medal of Science ceremony on 7 October 2009, Obama quoted the sentence as Sagan’s own description of his enthusiasm for discovery — preserved in the official White House transcript ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Sharon Begley, the Newsweek reporter who wrote it as the kicker to a profile of Sagan in 1977 — and who confirmed decades later, in four words, that “The words were not Sagan’s” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why this one stings
lead: There is a particular irony here. Carl Sagan wrote the Baloney Detection Kit — a set of tools for spotting claims that arrive without evidence. The most quoted sentence in his name is a claim that arrives without evidence. Cornell’s Carl Sagan Institute ↗, which uses that very kit to examine the line, lands on a wistful verdict: “Shame he never said it.”

It stuck because it is good — and because it sounds exactly like him. That is precisely the failure mode Sagan warned about: plausibility doing the work that citation should. A sentence written to sound like Sagan, printed inches from his photograph, needed only one careless reader to move it inside quotation marks. Nobody checked for thirty years.
detailsBody: The mechanism is mundane and worth naming, because it manufactures fake quotes at scale. Profile journalism routinely closes in the writer’s voice, summarising the subject’s outlook in language more lyrical than the subject actually used. Strip that paragraph from its page — as a columnist, a wire editor, or a screenshot does — and the surrounding cues that marked it as the reporter’s vanish. The words remain next to a famous name, and the name absorbs them.

Begley’s account adds the detail that makes it inevitable: Newsweek forbade ending a story on a quote. Writers were paid to invent the closing line. The house style that produced this sentence guaranteed it would be original to the reporter — and the same style guaranteed it would appear, unmarked, in the one position readers most associate with a subject’s last word.
context.pull: A sentence written about Sagan became a sentence by Sagan — the whole distance travelled on a pair of missing quotation marks.
